# What to Know Before Starting a GLP-1 Medicine

Deciding to start a weight-loss medicine can bring relief, questions, and some nerves. You may have heard about someone else's results and wondered what the experience would be like for you. Before the first dose, it helps to understand how treatment will fit into your health and everyday life.

This article covers adult weight management, using semaglutide (Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Zepbound) as examples. Instructions depend on the product prescribed. [Wegovy prescribing information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Zepbound prescribing information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

## Start with your health history and goals

For weight management, clinicians commonly consider prescription medicine for adults with a body mass index, or BMI, of 30 or higher, or 27 or higher with a weight-related condition such as high blood pressure. Meeting a threshold starts the assessment; your health history, other medicines, and treatment goals also matter. [NIDDK guidance](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/weight-management/prescription-medications-treat-overweight-obesity)

Be specific about what you hope will change. Is weight affecting your ability to move comfortably? Are you hoping to improve a health condition? That conversation gives you and your clinician something meaningful to revisit as treatment progresses.

Bring a complete list of prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, and supplements. Mention past pancreatitis, gallbladder or kidney problems, severe stomach-emptying problems, diabetes-related eye disease, and medication allergies. These details can change the assessment and monitoring plan. [Semaglutide patient information](https://medlineplus.gov/druginfo/meds/a618008.html)

Wegovy and Zepbound must not be used if you have a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (a specific thyroid cancer), or if you have multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN2). A previous serious allergic reaction to a medicine's active ingredient or other ingredients also rules that product out. Ask your clinician how any thyroid diagnosis or medication allergy affects treatment. [Wegovy contraindications](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Zepbound contraindications](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea for diabetes, the clinician may need to adjust treatment to reduce the risk of low blood sugar. Ask what to watch for and how to respond. [Wegovy precautions](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf)

Check for overlapping medicines, too. Wegovy and Zepbound should not be combined with another product containing the same active ingredient or with another GLP-1 receptor agonist. Make sure the prescriber knows about any weight-loss or diabetes treatment you already use. [Wegovy limitations of use](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Zepbound limitations of use](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

## Discuss pregnancy plans before treatment starts

Discuss pregnancy plans and breastfeeding before starting. These medicines should not be used for weight loss during pregnancy. Breastfeeding advice depends on the product and formulation: Wegovy's label specifically advises against breastfeeding during treatment with its tablets. Discuss an appropriate treatment and feeding plan with your clinician. [Wegovy pregnancy and breastfeeding guidance](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Zepbound pregnancy and breastfeeding guidance](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

For planned pregnancy, Wegovy's prescribing information says to stop it at least two months beforehand. [Wegovy planning guidance](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf)

Zepbound can reduce the effectiveness of oral hormonal birth control. Its label advises switching to a nonoral method or adding a barrier method for **four weeks after starting and four weeks after each dose increase**. Discuss this with your clinician. [Zepbound contraception guidance](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

## The first dose is the beginning of a process

Treatment starts at a lower dose and increases gradually to help reduce gastrointestinal side effects. Discuss tolerability with your prescriber; do not speed up the increases yourself. [Wegovy dosing guidance](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Zepbound dosing guidance](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

Before leaving with the prescription, make sure you understand how to take or administer your exact product, how to store it, and what to do about a missed dose. Have the pharmacist walk you through anything unclear. Keep the product's instructions somewhere you can find them again.

Tell any surgery or anesthesia team that you use the medicine. Delayed stomach emptying can matter during anesthesia or deep sedation. [Zepbound procedure precautions](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

## Less hunger still requires a plan for eating

If your appetite becomes smaller, the food you do eat still needs to provide enough nourishment. A joint advisory from four medical and nutrition organizations emphasizes assessing nutrition before treatment, preventing nutrient deficiencies, and combining adequate protein with strength training to help preserve muscle. [Joint nutrition advisory summary](https://www.obesity.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Joint_Nutritional-Priorities-to-Support-GLP-1-Therapy-for-Obesity.pdf)

Ask what that could look like with your food preferences, budget, and physical abilities. A dietitian can help tailor the plan if one is available to you. Tell the care team if eating becomes difficult or you are repeatedly skipping meals because you feel unwell.

## Know which symptoms need help

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation are possible side effects. Contact your clinician if symptoms are severe or do not settle. Repeated vomiting, trouble keeping fluids down, or reduced urination need prompt attention because dehydration can become serious. [Patient information and precautions](https://medlineplus.gov/druginfo/meds/a618008.html)

Persistent, severe abdominal pain—especially pain spreading to the back, with or without vomiting—needs urgent medical assessment. Trouble breathing or swelling of the tongue or throat calls for emergency help. These are examples, not a complete warning list; read the Medication Guide supplied with your prescription. [Serious symptoms](https://medlineplus.gov/druginfo/meds/a618008.html)

## Make a plan for the months after the first prescription

Ask when the first follow-up will happen, who handles questions between visits, and how you will assess progress together. Include the practical side: what insurance covers, the ongoing medicine cost, and whether appointments or tests add separate charges. Coverage varies, so check your own plan. [NIDDK treatment guidance](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/weight-management/prescription-medications-treat-overweight-obesity)

Know what product you are receiving and which pharmacy supplies it. FDA recommends a prescription from a doctor and a state-licensed pharmacy; compounded medicines do not undergo FDA approval for safety, effectiveness, and quality before marketing. [FDA guidance](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fdas-concerns-unapproved-glp-1-drugs-used-weight-loss)

Weight-management medicine may be a long-term treatment, and some weight regain is likely after stopping. Discuss affordability and continuity early, including what you would do if treatment became unavailable. [NIDDK guidance on duration](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/weight-management/prescription-medications-treat-overweight-obesity)

You should leave the starting conversation knowing how to take the medicine, who to contact with a problem, and when you will check in again. Those arrangements make the first prescription part of an ongoing care plan.

# How to Choose a Telehealth Weight-Loss Service

A polished website can make several weight-loss services look almost identical: a quick intake, a monthly price, medication delivered to your door.

The differences become clearer when you ask what happens after the first order. Who is responsible for your care? Who answers when side effects appear? What exactly is being prescribed, and which pharmacy supplies it?

Those questions are more useful than comparing promises about how quickly you can start. This guide is a way to assess a service, rather than a ranking of providers.

## Find the clinician behind the platform

A company’s brand name is not the name of the professional treating you. Look for an identifiable clinician, credentials you can verify, and a clear explanation of the clinical practice providing care.

The clinician must be authorized to treat you where you are located. State rules differ, and authorization can involve a state license, a compact, or another recognized pathway. The [HHS guide to telehealth licensure](https://telehealth.hhs.gov/licensure/licensing-across-state-lines) explains those distinctions.

Ask how to verify that authorization through the relevant professional licensing board. If you travel or move, tell the service; location can affect how care is provided.

An impressive biography or a picture of a person in a white coat is not the same as a verifiable treating professional.

## Look for an assessment that can lead to “no”

A prescribing evaluation should establish whether treatment is appropriate. Be cautious if a medicine appears guaranteed before your health history has been considered.

Ask how the service reviews your current medicines, relevant conditions, previous treatment, and pregnancy plans when applicable. Also ask when it recommends an in-person examination or testing. The appropriate assessment depends on the person; a particular number of laboratory tests is not a universal quality score.

The [FDA’s guidance on telehealth red flags](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fdas-concerns-unapproved-glp-1-drugs-used-weight-loss) warns about companies supplying medication without appropriate screening and a prescription, or without a clinician available afterward.

Before signing up, you should be able to understand how an actual clinical decision gets made.

## Identify both the medicine and the pharmacy

Ask for the medicine’s name, ingredient, formulation, and whether it is FDA-approved or compounded. “GLP-1 program” is too vague to tell you what you would receive.

A compounded medicine is not an FDA-approved generic. If compounding is proposed, ask which individual medical need it addresses and which pharmacy prepares it. Our guide to [compounded and FDA-approved medicines](/blog/compounded-vs-approved-weight-loss-medicines) explains the distinction.

Verify the pharmacy using the state board’s own records. The [FDA’s online-pharmacy guidance](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/how-buy-medicines-safely-online-pharmacy) identifies prescription requirements, licensing, and access to a pharmacist as important checks. A badge displayed on a seller’s website is not a substitute for checking the underlying record.

## Read the price as a treatment budget

A headline monthly fee may describe membership rather than the complete cost of care. Ask for the total you could owe, including consultations, medicine, shipping, testing when needed, and follow-up.

Then ask what happens if you are not prescribed a medicine, insurance declines coverage, a shipment is delayed, or you cancel. Get the terms in writing before paying.

For a concrete comparison, imagine three ordinary months of care and one month with a problem. Would you pay extra for a clinician to discuss persistent nausea? Does a replacement shipment cost more? Is there a continuing membership charge while medication is unavailable?

These are planning questions, not predictions that a particular company will charge those fees. They help make an offer understandable before you commit.

## Follow-up should be easy to describe

Ask how you reach the care team, who answers clinical messages, and what response time the service promises. Find out what happens outside office hours and how urgent symptoms should be handled locally.

Routine messaging is not an emergency service. A good plan makes that boundary clear and tells you where to turn when waiting for an online reply would be inappropriate.

Also ask how records can be shared with your regular clinician, how medication changes are documented, and what happens if you leave the service. Read the privacy notice before sending sensitive information; look for clear explanations of how your data is used and whom to contact with concerns.

## Choose a care relationship you can understand

You do not need to become an expert in every telehealth business model. You do need clear answers about the clinician, medicine, pharmacy, cost, and ongoing support.

If those answers remain vague while the sales process stays effortless, pause before paying. The service should be able to explain the care as clearly as it explains how to subscribe.

articles.content:
# Compounded vs. FDA-Approved Weight-Loss Medicines

Two websites may advertise semaglutide at very different prices. One names an FDA-approved product. The other describes a compounded version, perhaps using phrases such as “personalized” or “same active ingredient.”

Those descriptions can sound interchangeable. They are not equivalent regulatory categories, and the distinction matters when you are deciding what would be prescribed and dispensed.

Compounding has legitimate medical uses. Understanding those uses also means understanding what FDA approval does—and does not—tell you about a particular product.

## Start with the finished medicine

FDA approval applies to a specific drug product and its approved uses. A compounded preparation does not become an FDA-approved product simply because an approved medicine contains the same named ingredient.

The FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness, and quality before they are marketed. That does not mean every compounded medicine is harmful. It means the assurance provided by the drug approval process is absent. [FDA compounding questions and answers](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/compounding-and-fda-questions-and-answers).

An FDA-approved generic is different again: it has gone through the applicable FDA approval pathway. Calling a compounded product a “generic” can obscure this distinction.

## Why compounding exists

A person may need a formulation an approved product cannot provide—for example, one without an ingredient they are allergic to. In appropriate circumstances, compounding can meet an individual medical need.

But the reason needs to be specific. The FDA recommends using compounded drugs when a patient’s medical needs cannot be met by an approved drug. There are also rules affecting compounding during drug shortages; an old shortage-related advertisement does not establish that a product can lawfully be compounded today.

Ask the prescriber what need the proposed preparation addresses, whether an approved option can meet it, and what evidence supports the choice. The answer should describe your care, rather than relying only on the word “custom.”

## The label needs to explain what you are getting

For compounded GLP-1 products, the FDA has reported concerns involving dosing mistakes, products with misleading pharmacy information, and forms of semaglutide that differ from the ingredient used in approved products. In particular, semaglutide sodium and semaglutide acetate are different active ingredients from the base form used in approved medicines. [FDA concerns about unapproved GLP-1 drugs](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fdas-concerns-unapproved-glp-1-drugs-used-weight-loss).

If a prescription comes in a vial, understand that milligrams, milliliters, and syringe “units” are different measurements. A volume instruction cannot be carried from one concentration to another as if the amount of medicine stayed the same.

Have the dispensing pharmacist explain the exact preparation and demonstrate how its instructions match the supplied device. Do not borrow a dosing chart from a social-media group or reuse instructions from a different product.

## Check who actually prepared and dispensed it

The name on the marketing website may differ from the pharmacy name. Ask for the dispensing pharmacy and, when relevant, the compounder. Verify the pharmacy through the state board rather than relying solely on a logo or seal.

The [FDA’s online-pharmacy guidance](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/how-buy-medicines-safely-online-pharmacy) also recommends checking for a valid prescription requirement and a pharmacist who can answer questions.

When medication arrives, unresolved problems with the label, instructions, packaging, or storage conditions should be addressed before use. The FDA specifically advises against using injectable GLP-1 drugs that arrive warm or without adequate refrigeration. Contact the pharmacy and prescribing team rather than guessing that a questionable shipment is fine.

## Retatrutide is a separate issue

As of October 19, 2026, the FDA states that retatrutide is not a component of an FDA-approved drug and cannot be used in compounding under federal law. An online seller calling it “compounded” or “research use only” does not turn it into an approved treatment.

Clinical research and retail availability are different things. Our [retatrutide explainer](/blog/what-is-retatrutide) discusses the compound’s research status and why that distinction matters.

## Make the comparison before making the purchase

Price can be a real barrier, and wanting an affordable option is reasonable. A useful conversation still needs the full medicine name, approval status, pharmacy identity, clinical reason for the prescription, and a way to get help.

If you are already receiving a compounded medicine, bring those details to your prescriber or pharmacist. This article cannot determine the quality or appropriateness of your individual preparation.

The immediate goal is a clear account of what you are taking and why. You should not have to infer that from advertising language.

articles.content:
# Do GLP-1 Medicines Cause Muscle Loss?

A falling number on the scale does not tell you exactly what you have lost. That is why headlines about muscle loss during GLP-1 treatment can be both worrying and confusing.

Some lean tissue can be lost as body weight falls. The important questions are how much, what the measurement actually represents, and whether your strength and everyday function are being protected.

It helps to separate three things often treated as interchangeable: weight, lean mass, and muscle.

## What “lean mass” actually means

A body-composition scan divides the body into categories. In a DXA scan, lean soft tissue includes more than skeletal muscle; it also includes water and other nonfat soft tissues. Bone mineral is measured separately.

So a study reporting a reduction in lean mass has not directly measured the same percentage loss of muscle. Nor has it necessarily measured a loss of strength. Those are related questions that require different assessments. The [SURMOUNT-1 body-composition study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11965027/) defines these measures and discusses their limitations.

This distinction matters when a dramatic headline turns a scan result into a prediction about what will happen to your body.

## What one tirzepatide study found

In a substudy of SURMOUNT-1, researchers analyzed body-composition scans from 160 adults with obesity or overweight, without type 2 diabetes. They compared pooled tirzepatide doses with placebo over 72 weeks.

About three-quarters of the weight lost in the tirzepatide group was fat mass and about one-quarter was lean mass. The proportions were similar in the placebo group, although the tirzepatide group lost substantially more weight overall.

That does **not** mean participants lost one-quarter of their starting muscle. It describes how the lost weight was divided between measurement categories.

The study was funded by Eli Lilly, tirzepatide’s manufacturer. It involved a relatively small subset of the larger trial and did not directly test muscle strength. Its [published correction](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12710557/) fixes the units on a subgroup graph; the overall fat-versus-lean proportions above are reported in the study’s results.

These findings help explain what happened in that group. They cannot predict an individual’s muscle changes or establish that all GLP-1 medicines have identical effects.

## Strength is part of the treatment conversation

The ability to carry groceries, rise from a chair, climb stairs, or move comfortably matters alongside weight. A smaller body is not the only goal.

The [joint nutrition advisory on GLP-1 treatment](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12304835/) recommends attention to food intake, resistance exercise, and physical function. Older adults and people who already have low strength or difficulty eating may need particular support.

This does not mean every person needs a scan or an expensive gym membership. It means your care team should hear about changes in what you can do. New difficulty with stairs or getting out of a chair is useful information, even if you are pleased with the scale.

## Food and movement work together

When appetite drops, it can take planning to get enough food and protein. A pattern of skipping meals and relying on a few bites at dinner is worth discussing. Our guide to [eating with a smaller appetite](/blog/what-to-eat-on-glp-1) offers practical starting points.

Resistance exercise asks muscles to work against a load. Depending on your ability, that might involve bands, weights, machines, or modified body-weight movements. The CDC recommends muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days a week for adults, alongside aerobic activity; people with health limitations can adapt activity with professional guidance. [CDC adult activity guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/guidelines/adults.html).

There is no need to begin with an ambitious routine. Ask what is safe and realistic for your joints, balance, experience, and health. A physical therapist or qualified exercise professional can help when movement is difficult.

Neither a protein target nor an exercise program guarantees that no lean tissue will be lost. The purpose is to support strength and function while treatment is adjusted to your needs.

## Bring changes in function to follow-up

If you feel progressively weaker, unusually exhausted, or unable to eat enough, tell your clinician. Do not assume that weakness proves muscle loss—or that it is an unavoidable price of treatment. Symptoms need their own assessment.

A useful follow-up conversation can include weight, eating, activity, and one or two everyday tasks that matter to you. “I can walk farther, but lifting the shopping bags has become harder” tells a clinician more than the scale alone.

You deserve a treatment plan that pays attention to the person moving through daily life, as well as the number being recorded.

articles.content:
# GLP-1 Pills vs. Injections: What’s Different?

If a weight-loss medicine comes as a pill, does that make the decision simple? For someone who dislikes needles, it may seem that way.

The route matters, but so do the ingredient, approved use, daily routine, other medicines, and side effects. Two pills can have more practical differences than a pill and an injection.

The options have also changed. This overview reflects US product information checked on October 19, 2026.

## There is more than one kind of pill

Wegovy contains semaglutide and is available in tablet and injection formulations. Foundayo contains orforglipron, a different GLP-1 receptor agonist. The FDA approved Foundayo in April 2026 for long-term weight management in eligible adults, alongside diet and physical activity. [FDA Foundayo approval announcement](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-new-molecular-entity-under-national-priority-voucher-program).

Zepbound contains tirzepatide, which acts at both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. It is an injectable medicine. Grouping these treatments under “GLP-1s” can be convenient, but it should not hide their differences.

Here is how the routine differs for these examples:

| Product | Ingredient and route | Basic schedule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wegovy tablets | Oral semaglutide | Once daily; specific fasting and water instructions |
| Foundayo | Oral orforglipron | Once daily, with or without food |
| Wegovy injection | Injected semaglutide | Once weekly |
| Zepbound | Injected tirzepatide | Once weekly |

Sources: [Wegovy prescribing information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Foundayo prescribing information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/foundayo-uspi.pdf), and [Zepbound prescribing information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf). This table describes routines, not dose equivalence or a complete list of treatments.

## A morning routine can become part of treatment

Wegovy tablets must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach with no more than four ounces of plain water. The instructions require waiting at least 30 minutes before food, other drinks, or other oral medicines.

Foundayo does not have that fasting requirement. It can be taken with or without food.

Imagine someone who takes several medicines with breakfast and leaves for work early. The difference could matter more than simply preferring a tablet. It is worth asking the pharmacist to fit the actual instructions into your routine before assuming that any oral option will be easy.

A weekly injection has a different set of practical tasks: learning the device, following storage instructions, and remembering the scheduled day.

## Milligrams are not a strength ranking

The number printed on one product cannot be used to calculate an equivalent amount of another. Different ingredients and formulations reach and act in the body differently.

Even when two products contain semaglutide, switching routes requires the product-specific prescribing plan. Do not substitute tablets for injections, combine them, or adjust amounts using an online conversion.

If you are considering a change because of travel, needle discomfort, side effects, or access, explain that reason. The prescriber can assess whether the proposed alternative is suitable and how a transition should work.

## A pill can still have substantial precautions

Avoiding an injection does not remove the possibility of gastrointestinal or other serious adverse effects. The FDA’s Foundayo announcement, for example, includes warnings about pancreatitis, dehydration-related kidney injury, severe digestive reactions, and other risks.

Foundayo also has specific interactions with other drugs, and its label advises additional or non-oral contraception for 30 days after starting and after each dose increase for people using oral contraceptives. Do not apply that interval to another product: the instructions differ.

All four examples in the table have important contraindications and warnings, including restrictions involving a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, a particular thyroid cancer, or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2). Pregnancy plans, breastfeeding, other medicines, and digestive conditions need a prescribing discussion.

Our [side-effects guide](/blog/glp-1-side-effects) explains symptoms that should prompt help. It does not replace your specific Medication Guide.

## Compare the treatment that fits your situation

The easiest option to take is not necessarily the most appropriate one for your health, and a trial percentage from one study cannot establish which product would work best for you.

Ask what benefit is expected for your circumstances, what evidence supports that expectation, what follow-up is included, and what the complete cost will be. Check the exact product and formulation covered by any insurance or access arrangement.

You can have a strong preference about pills or injections. The best conversation starts with that preference and then checks whether the treatment behind it fits.

articles.content:
# GLP-1 Side Effects: What’s Common and When to Get Help

When you start a medicine, “some stomach upset is common” can be a frustratingly vague instruction. Does that mean a little nausea after breakfast, or a day when you cannot keep water down?

Those situations need different responses.

GLP-1-based medicines can cause digestive symptoms, particularly around starting treatment or increasing a dose. Some symptoms are manageable; others need prompt assessment. This guide focuses on recognizing the difference, with examples from semaglutide and tirzepatide. Your own product’s Medication Guide remains the reference for its specific risks.

## Common does not mean you have to put up with it

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and abdominal discomfort appear in the prescribing information for both Wegovy and Zepbound. Frequency and severity differ between people and products. [Wegovy information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf); [Zepbound information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf).

Tell your care team if symptoms interfere with eating, drinking, sleep, or ordinary activities. You do not need to wait until something becomes an emergency to ask for help.

A brief description is useful: when the symptom started, whether a dose changed recently, how often it happens, and whether you can eat and drink. “Nausea” alone gives less information than “I have felt sick after every meal since the increase and have barely managed fluids today.”

## Smaller meals may help mild symptoms

When nausea is mild, smaller portions and eating more slowly may be easier than a large meal. Rich or fatty foods may be harder to tolerate. For constipation, fluids and a gradual increase in fiber can be useful, depending on your health and symptoms.

The [joint nutrition advisory for GLP-1 treatment](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12304835/) discusses these approaches, while emphasizing early contact with the prescribing team when symptoms develop. They are supportive measures, not a substitute for assessing severe or persistent symptoms.

Ask before adding laxatives, anti-nausea medicines, or supplements. Your medical history and other medicines affect what is appropriate. Do not accelerate a dose increase or change the schedule yourself.

## Symptoms that need prompt medical attention

**Severe abdominal pain that does not go away**, especially if it spreads toward the back, needs urgent assessment. Wegovy and Zepbound Medication Guides advise stopping the medicine and calling the healthcare provider right away for this pattern because it can indicate pancreatitis.

**Upper abdominal pain with fever, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or pale stools** can signal a gallbladder problem. Contact a healthcare professional promptly.

**Repeated vomiting or diarrhea, inability to keep fluids down, much less urination, or marked dizziness** should not be dismissed as routine adjustment. Fluid loss can become serious. Seek urgent care if symptoms are severe or you cannot reach your clinician.

These patterns are described in the product information linked above and in [MedlinePlus’s semaglutide patient guidance](https://medlineplus.gov/druginfo/meds/a618008.html). You do not need to diagnose the cause before seeking help.

## When to seek emergency help

Trouble breathing, swelling of the tongue or throat, collapse, or a severe allergic reaction requires emergency help. In the United States, call 911.

Low blood glucose is another concern, especially when a GLP-1-based medicine is used with insulin or a sulfonylurea. Ask your diabetes team for a plan before symptoms occur. Shakiness, sweating, confusion, or unusual weakness may be warning signs. Seizure or loss of consciousness needs emergency treatment. If a prescribed glucagon rescue medicine is available, someone trained to use it should follow your emergency plan and call 911. [NIDDK guidance on low blood glucose](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/preventing-problems/low-blood-glucose-hypoglycemia).

## A few symptoms and situations deserve their own conversation

Report new vision changes, a neck lump, persistent hoarseness, or swallowing difficulty promptly. These are among the concerns addressed in the product guides; they should not be explained away as ordinary stomach side effects.

Tell a surgery or procedure team that you take the medicine, including before anesthesia or deep sedation. Do not choose your own stopping interval. The team needs to plan around your treatment and procedure.

For Wegovy or Zepbound being used for weight management, the labels instruct patients to stop treatment when pregnancy is recognized and contact the healthcare provider. A future pregnancy plan belongs in the conversation before treatment as well.

## Leave follow-up with a usable plan

Before the next dose change, know how to reach the clinical team and what to do outside office hours. Ask which symptoms should trigger a call and which should send you directly for urgent help.

For mild symptoms, the plan might include food changes and closer follow-up. For more serious problems, it may involve a different treatment decision. The goal is care you can safely live with—not proving how much discomfort you can tolerate.

# How GLP-1 Weight-Loss Medicines Work

Hunger can make a simple instruction—eat a little less—feel anything but simple. You may know what you intended to eat and still finish a meal wanting more.

GLP-1 medicines act on signals involved in appetite. For some people, treatment can mean feeling less hungry and more satisfied after eating. That change helps explain how medication can make a difference when advice about food has not been enough. [Research on appetite and semaglutide](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7898914/)

## Your body already makes GLP-1

GLP-1 stands for glucagon-like peptide-1. It is a hormone your intestines release in response to food. Among its jobs, it helps the pancreas release insulin when blood sugar rises and influences how quickly food leaves the stomach. These effects helped make GLP-1 a target for diabetes treatment. [NIH explanation](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/news/archive/2021/story-discovery-medications-diabetes-obesity-emerged-research-pancreatic-hormone)

The hormone also influences appetite. Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors—the parts of cells that receive the signal. These receptors are found in brain regions involved in appetite regulation. Semaglutide reduces calorie intake, an effect thought to work through appetite. [Wegovy prescribing information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf)

The body's own GLP-1 breaks down quickly. Medicines were developed to keep acting for longer, making sustained treatment possible. This is why the treatment can influence eating beyond the brief hormonal response to a single meal. [NIH explanation](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/news/archive/2021/story-discovery-medications-diabetes-obesity-emerged-research-pancreatic-hormone)

## Why eating can feel different

Researchers have studied appetite as well as weight. In a small, 20-week randomized trial involving 72 adults with obesity, people receiving weekly semaglutide injections, gradually increased to 2.4 mg, reported less hunger and greater fullness than those receiving placebo. They also reported fewer or weaker food cravings. The study was funded by the manufacturer, Novo Nordisk. [Read the study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7898914/)

For someone who responds that way, stopping a meal can feel easier because the desire to keep eating has changed. That is a different experience from deciding to stop while still feeling hungry. The findings help explain a possible treatment experience; they do not mean everyone will feel the same change.

These medicines can also slow the movement of food out of the stomach. That is one part of their action, but it does not explain everything about weight loss. For example, tirzepatide's prescribing information says this slowing is greatest after the first dose and diminishes over time. [Zepbound prescribing information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

## The names describe different medicines

Wegovy contains semaglutide, which activates GLP-1 receptors. Zepbound contains tirzepatide, which activates both GLP-1 and another hormone receptor called GIP. Their prescribing details differ. [Wegovy information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Zepbound information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

Wegovy is available as injections and tablets. The formulation matters: the ingredient name alone does not tell you how a product is used. [Wegovy information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf)

Retatrutide also appears in discussions of weight-loss medicines. As of October 19, 2026, it remains investigational and is not FDA-approved. Research interest should not be confused with an approved treatment being available. [FDA guidance](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fdas-concerns-unapproved-glp-1-drugs-used-weight-loss)

## What those changes can mean for weight

In the 68-week STEP 1 trial, 1,961 adults without diabetes who had obesity, or overweight with a weight-related health condition, received weekly semaglutide injections at a target dose of 2.4 mg or placebo. The estimated average weight loss was 14.9% with semaglutide and 2.4% with placebo. Both groups received lifestyle support. This manufacturer-funded trial tested a particular regimen; its average is not a forecast for an individual or for every GLP-1 product. [STEP 1 trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33567185/)

Side effects also matter. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation are common with semaglutide and tirzepatide. Serious risks include pancreatitis, gallbladder problems, and dehydration-related kidney injury. Certain histories rule them out, including a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or having MEN 2, a rare inherited condition. A previous serious allergic reaction to a product's ingredients also rules that product out. [Wegovy information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Zepbound information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

## Treatment involves more than a prescription

A clinician needs to consider medical history, other medicines, pregnancy plans, likely benefits, and costs. Nutrition, physical activity, and follow-up remain part of care. Treatment may continue long term if it is helping and the risks remain acceptable; some weight regain is common after stopping. [NIDDK treatment guidance](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/weight-management/prescription-medications-treat-overweight-obesity)

Before starting, it is worth understanding what follow-up will look like: who will help with side effects, how progress will be assessed, and what happens if the treatment is difficult to tolerate or afford. Those conversations connect the science of appetite to the practical question of whether a medicine fits your life.

articles.content:
# Insulin Resistance, Explained Without the Jargon

“Insulin resistance” turns up in conversations about weight, blood sugar, and metabolism so often that it can begin to sound like an explanation for everything.

It describes something specific: the body is not responding to insulin as well as it should. It can increase the risk of prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, but those terms are not interchangeable.

Understanding the difference helps you make sense of a test result—and avoid diagnosing yourself from a symptom list online.

## What insulin normally does

Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas. Among its jobs, it helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells where it can be used for energy.

With insulin resistance, cells in tissues such as muscle, fat, and liver respond less effectively to the insulin signal. The pancreas may compensate by making more insulin. Blood glucose can remain within its usual range for a time; if the system cannot keep up, glucose levels rise.

That is why insulin resistance does not automatically mean a person already has diabetes. The [NIDDK’s insulin resistance guide](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/what-is-diabetes/prediabetes-insulin-resistance) explains the relationship between the underlying process and higher blood glucose.

## Prediabetes describes blood glucose, not a body type

Prediabetes means blood glucose is above the normal range but below the range used to diagnose diabetes. It signals increased risk, rather than a certainty that diabetes will develop.

Body weight and waist size can be part of a risk assessment, but appearance cannot tell you a blood glucose result. Family history, age, physical activity, a history of gestational diabetes, some health conditions, and certain medicines can also matter.

People with insulin resistance or prediabetes often have no symptoms. That makes claims that a particular craving, body shape, or tired afternoon proves insulin resistance unreliable.

If you are concerned, ask about your risk and whether testing is appropriate. You do not need to identify a visible sign before having that conversation.

## What the usual tests actually measure

Clinicians commonly assess blood glucose using tests such as A1C or fasting plasma glucose. An oral glucose tolerance test is another option in some circumstances.

A1C reflects average blood glucose over roughly the previous three months. Fasting glucose measures the level at the time the sample is taken after the required fast. Neither is a direct measurement of how much insulin resistance a person has.

For many nonpregnant adults, an A1C from **5.7% to 6.4%** falls in the prediabetes range. A result of **6.5% or above** is in the diabetes range, but diagnosis generally needs confirmation when clear symptoms are absent. Conditions affecting red blood cells or hemoglobin can make A1C misleading, so a clinician needs to interpret the result in context. [NIDDK A1C guidance](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diagnostic-tests/a1c-test).

Specialized testing of insulin resistance is used mainly in research. An online “optimal insulin” target should not replace an assessment of your overall health.

## A useful response is broader than cutting out sugar

Food matters, but the conversation should not end with a single forbidden ingredient. Activity, sleep, weight management when appropriate, and treatment of related conditions can all be part of care.

You might begin by asking which change would be most useful and manageable for you. That could mean working on a regular eating pattern, replacing a usual sugary drink, finding an activity you can sustain, or getting help with a sleep problem. These are examples to discuss, not a prescription for every reader.

The NIDDK describes lifestyle support and, for some people, medicines such as metformin as ways to reduce diabetes risk. Its [Diabetes Prevention Program overview](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/about-niddk/research-areas/diabetes/diabetes-prevention-program-dpp) explains the research behind prevention efforts.

You do not need to achieve an idealized routine before beginning. A plan is more useful when it accounts for your work, food access, mobility, and preferences.

## Where weight-loss medicines fit

A concern about insulin resistance alone does not tell you which medicine you need. Eligibility and treatment choice depend on the diagnosis, weight-related health concerns, other medicines, and individual risks.

If GLP-1-based treatment comes up, ask what condition the clinician is treating and what improvement will be measured. Is the goal blood glucose management, weight management, or another approved use? The ingredient and brand name are not enough to answer that question.

For background, our guide to [how GLP-1 weight-loss medicines work](/blog/how-glp-1-weight-loss-medicines-work) explains the treatment family.

## Leave with a result you understand

If a test is abnormal, ask what it means, whether it needs confirmation, and when it should be repeated. Also ask what you can reasonably work on before the next visit.

A laboratory number is information for making a plan. It is not a verdict on your effort, and it does not tell the whole story of your health.

articles.content:
# Semaglutide vs. Tirzepatide: What’s the Difference?

If you have started reading about weight-loss medicines, you have probably encountered several names before getting a clear explanation of how they fit together. Semaglutide. Tirzepatide. Wegovy. Zepbound. Then someone mentions Ozempic or Mounjaro, and the list gets longer.

The names become easier to follow once you separate the active ingredient from the brand. From there, you can look at the questions that matter: how the medicines work, what researchers have found, and what could make one a better fit for your health and daily life.

## Two ingredients, several brand names

Semaglutide is the active ingredient in Wegovy. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Zepbound. Both brands have approved uses for weight management. [Wegovy information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Zepbound information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

The same ingredients also appear in medicines approved for type 2 diabetes: semaglutide in Ozempic and tirzepatide in Mounjaro. Sharing an ingredient does not make every branded product's dose or approved uses interchangeable. [Ozempic information](https://www.novo-pi.com/ozempic.pdf), [Mounjaro information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/mounjaro-uspi.pdf)

Semaglutide activates receptors for GLP-1, a hormone involved in blood sugar and appetite regulation. Tirzepatide activates GLP-1 receptors and receptors for another hormone, GIP. Both medicines can reduce food intake through effects on appetite. [Semaglutide mechanism](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [tirzepatide mechanism](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

That gives researchers a reason to study the medicines separately. Counting hormone targets, by itself, cannot tell you how much weight someone will lose.

## What happened when researchers compared them directly?

The SURMOUNT-5 trial randomly assigned 751 adults without type 2 diabetes to weekly injections of tirzepatide or semaglutide for 72 weeks. Treatment reached the highest dose each participant could tolerate within the study's selected doses. [Published study abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40353578/)

| Treatment studied | Estimated average weight loss at 72 weeks (% of starting weight) |
| --- | --- |
| Semaglutide, 1.7 or 2.4 mg weekly | 13.7% |
| Tirzepatide, 10 or 15 mg weekly | 20.2% |

Tirzepatide produced the larger average reduction: a difference of 6.5 percentage points. The analysis accounted for participants who stopped their assigned treatment; these are estimated group averages, not individual targets or promises. [SURMOUNT-5 results](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40353578/), [analysis definition](https://investor.lilly.com/node/52376)

Participants had obesity, or overweight with a weight-related health condition, and both groups received diet and physical-activity counseling. Eli Lilly, which makes tirzepatide, funded the trial. It was open-label, meaning participants and investigators knew which treatment was being used. [Study details](https://investor.lilly.com/node/52376)

The doses matter when interpreting the result. This trial did not compare tirzepatide with oral semaglutide or the newer 7.2 mg Wegovy injection. Those are different regimens included in current Wegovy labeling. The result answers the comparison that was tested. [Trial methods](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40353578/), [current Wegovy information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf)

## Some differences show up in everyday treatment

Wegovy comes as a weekly injection or a daily tablet. The tablet has specific instructions about taking it on an empty stomach and waiting before eating, drinking, or taking other oral medicines. Zepbound is a weekly injection. A preference for tablets is worth discussing alongside the routine they require. [Wegovy information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Zepbound information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

Other health conditions can influence the conversation, too. Wegovy has an FDA-approved use to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death, heart attack, and stroke in adults with established cardiovascular disease and either overweight or obesity. [FDA cardiovascular approval](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-treatment-reduce-risk-serious-heart-problems-specifically-adults-obesity-or)

Zepbound has an approved use for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. [FDA sleep-apnea approval](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-medication-obstructive-sleep-apnea)

Those are examples of why a clinician looks beyond the weight-loss percentage. An approval for a particular condition also does not prove that one medicine is better than the other for every related health outcome.

## Side effects belong in the comparison

Both medicines commonly cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. Serious risks include pancreatitis, gallbladder problems, and kidney injury related to dehydration. Neither should be used by someone with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or with MEN 2, a rare inherited condition. A previous serious allergic reaction to a product's ingredients also rules that product out. [Wegovy safety information](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf), [Zepbound safety information](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

One specific difference concerns birth-control pills. Tirzepatide can reduce the effectiveness of oral hormonal contraceptives. Its label advises switching to a non-oral method or adding a barrier method for four weeks after starting and four weeks after each dose increase. Discuss that plan with the prescriber before treatment. [Zepbound contraception guidance](https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf)

## Choosing something you can continue

The decision also involves other medicines, pregnancy plans, cost, and follow-up. Insurance coverage varies, so checking your own plan is more useful than assuming one brand will be affordable. Weight-management treatment may continue long term when it is helping and its risks remain acceptable. [NIDDK treatment guidance](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/weight-management/prescription-medications-treat-overweight-obesity)

Before starting, ask what improvement you and your clinician are aiming for, how side effects will be handled, and what happens if the medicine becomes difficult to obtain or afford. Those answers help turn a comparison between two drugs into a workable plan for your care.

articles.content:
# Why Sleep Belongs in the Conversation About Appetite and Weight

After a short night, even an ordinary day can feel harder to manage. If food seems more distracting or satisfying meals feel harder to plan, the conversation does not have to begin and end with willpower.

Sleep is involved in appetite regulation, and too little sleep can leave people feeling hungrier. That makes sleep worth discussing when you are trying to understand eating patterns. It does not make an extra hour in bed a guaranteed weight-loss treatment. [NIH: How sleep affects health](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep-deprivation/health-effects)

## Appetite does not operate separately from sleep

Sleep helps regulate hormones involved in hunger and fullness. Inadequate sleep can also affect attention and decision-making. Those are different parts of the same practical problem: getting through a day while tired. [NIH: How sleep affects health](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep-deprivation/health-effects)

It can be useful to notice the setting around a difficult eating day. Was there an early shift, a child awake overnight, or a long stretch of interrupted sleep? That observation is a starting point for a conversation. It cannot tell you that sleep caused a particular weight change or explain every craving.

## Better sleep is a health goal, not a weight-loss promise

Researchers are studying whether improving sleep can support weight management. A 2026 systematic review included different approaches, including sleep extension and approaches involving insomnia therapy or sleep hygiene. Its findings varied by intervention: the pooled BMI change for sleep-extension studies was not statistically significant. The studies excluded people with obstructive sleep apnea. [Read the review abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42044907/)

That distinction matters. Evidence about one sleep intervention in one group should not become a promise that everyone will lose weight by sleeping longer. Nor should it turn into a reason to ignore a persistent sleep problem if your weight stays the same.

The NIH describes 7–9 hours a night as the usual recommendation for adults. Individual needs and circumstances vary, and more than nine hours is not automatically a problem—for example, during recovery from sleep loss or illness. [NIH: How much sleep is enough?](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep/how-much-sleep)

## Start with a change your life can accommodate

General sleep guidance includes keeping a reasonably consistent schedule, making the bedroom quiet and dark, and allowing a calmer period before bed. Caffeine can interfere with sleep for hours after you consume it. These are possible places to look, not a demand for a perfect evening routine. [NIH: Healthy sleep habits](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep-deprivation/healthy-sleep-habits)

For a shift worker, “go to bed earlier” may be meaningless. The NIH's guidance for shift work includes protecting daytime sleep from light and noise and limiting caffeine to the earlier part of a shift. Persistent difficulty sleeping deserves a conversation with a clinician. [NIH: Healthy sleep habits](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep-deprivation/healthy-sleep-habits)

An original one-week note can help organize that conversation. Record roughly when you tried to sleep, when you woke, whether sleep was interrupted, and how rested you felt. Add a short note about daytime hunger only if it is useful to you. This is an observation aid, not a diagnostic test or another score to chase. Keep the note private and bring it to your care team if needed.

## When the issue may be more than a short night

Loud, frequent snoring, pauses in breathing, gasping during sleep, and daytime sleepiness can be signs of sleep apnea. Sometimes another person notices the nighttime symptoms first. Tell a healthcare professional about them; a symptom list alone cannot establish the diagnosis. [NIH: Sleep apnea symptoms](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep-apnea/symptoms)

If sleep has become a persistent struggle, it belongs in your healthcare conversation now. You do not need to prove that it changed your weight before asking for help with it.

articles.content:
# What Happens When You Stop a GLP-1 Medicine?

People stop weight-loss medicines for many reasons. The cost changes. Side effects become difficult. Pregnancy plans arise. Or they reach a point where they want to know whether the medicine is still necessary.

The question is reasonable. So is wanting a clear answer about what may happen afterward.

Weight regain is common after treatment stops, but studies describe averages, not a fixed outcome for every person. Planning the transition with your prescriber gives you a chance to address the reason for stopping and decide what support comes next. The [NIDDK’s overview of weight-management medicines](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/weight-management/prescription-medications-treat-overweight-obesity) describes treatment as potentially long term when benefits continue and side effects are acceptable.

## What withdrawal studies tell us

In an extension of the STEP 1 trial, 327 participants were followed after the trial’s semaglutide or placebo treatment ended. One year after stopping semaglutide, the group had regained roughly two-thirds of its earlier weight loss on average. Some weight loss remained. The structured lifestyle intervention also ended, so the study cannot isolate stopping the medicine from stopping that support. Novo Nordisk funded the research. [STEP 1 extension](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35441470/).

SURMOUNT-4 asked a related question using tirzepatide. After 36 weeks taking the medicine, 670 adults without diabetes were randomly assigned either to continue it or to switch to placebo. Diet and activity support continued.

Over the following 52 weeks, average body weight fell another 5.5% in the continued-treatment group and rose 14.0% in the placebo group. Those percentages use weight at the point of randomization as the starting point—not the amount of weight previously lost.

This Eli Lilly-funded trial included people who had completed the initial treatment period, so its results do not describe everyone who starts tirzepatide. [SURMOUNT-4 trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10714284/).

## Regain is not a measure of character

If appetite becomes harder to manage after a medicine is withdrawn, it can feel as though something you learned has vanished. It may be more helpful to recognize that the support provided by treatment has changed.

Weight management is influenced by biology as well as circumstances and behavior. Research on weight regulation describes increased appetite and changes in energy expenditure after weight loss. These pressures help explain why maintaining a lower weight can require ongoing support. [Research on the physiology of weight-loss plateaus](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38644683/).

That is different from saying regain is inevitable or that daily habits do not matter. It means a plan should account for the difficulty rather than treating any upward movement as a personal failure.

## The reason for stopping shapes the next step

Someone stopping because of a serious reaction needs a different plan from someone whose insurance coverage is ending. Tell your clinician which problem you are trying to solve.

If the issue is access, ask about appropriate treatment alternatives and continuity of care before the supply runs out. If eating or side effects have become difficult, describe those problems directly. A discussion about tolerability should not be reduced to whether you can endure another month.

Pregnancy planning and significant adverse effects require product-specific advice. Follow urgent instructions in your medicine’s Medication Guide when they apply; do not wait for a routine appointment to report a serious reaction.

## Make room for a maintenance plan

A useful plan covers follow-up, nourishment, activity, and what changes should prompt contact. If the medicine is also helping manage diabetes, ask how blood glucose will be monitored and how the rest of your treatment may need to change.

It can help to agree on a manageable way to watch the trend without turning every weigh-in into a judgment. Also track things that matter to you: energy, strength, eating patterns, and the health measures your clinician is following.

Do not improvise a taper, stretch injections, share medication, or restart an old dose after a break. Instructions vary by product and by the length of the interruption. Ask the prescriber or pharmacist for a specific plan; for example, the [Wegovy Medication Guide](https://www.novo-pi.com/wegovy.pdf) includes specific guidance on restarting after missed weeks.

## Does this mean treatment has to be forever?

The studies support taking long-term treatment seriously. They do not decide what every individual must do for the rest of their life.

Benefits, side effects, access, preferences, and health circumstances can change. Reassessment is part of care. A decision to continue should have a reason; a decision to stop should have a plan.

If you do regain weight, you can return to that conversation. There is no requirement to wait until all progress has been lost before asking for help.

articles.content:
# What BMI Can—and Cannot—Tell You

You open an appointment summary and see a number beside “BMI.” Underneath it is a category that sounds like a verdict. Before deciding what that label means about your health, it helps to understand what went into it.

Body mass index uses two measurements: height and weight. It can flag something worth discussing, but it cannot describe everything happening in your body. The useful next question is what other information belongs beside it. [CDC: About BMI](https://www.cdc.gov/bmi/about/index.html)

## What the calculation actually measures

BMI divides weight in kilograms by height in meters squared. It is a way to express weight relative to height. It does not directly measure body fat, distinguish fat from muscle and bone, or show where fat is carried. [CDC: About BMI](https://www.cdc.gov/bmi/about/index.html)

Here is a fictional example. Two adults are each 1.70 meters tall and weigh 80 kilograms. Both have a BMI of about 27.7: 80 divided by 1.70 squared. The calculation produces the same answer even if their muscle mass, blood pressure, medical histories, and daily lives differ. Those differences do not enter the formula.

That is why a BMI result cannot answer a question such as “How much of my weight is muscle?” The measurement simply does not contain that information.

## Why clinicians still use it

BMI is quick and inexpensive to obtain, and it helps identify weight categories associated with health risks. It is also useful for following population trends. Those uses give it a place in healthcare even though it is incomplete as an individual assessment. [CDC: About BMI](https://www.cdc.gov/bmi/about/index.html)

For adults age 20 and older, the CDC uses these categories:

| BMI | Category |
| --- | --- |
| Below 18.5 | Underweight |
| 18.5 to below 25 | Healthy weight |
| 25 to below 30 | Overweight |
| 30 or higher | Obesity |

These are screening categories. The words “healthy weight” describe the category; they do not establish that every aspect of a person's health is healthy. Children and teenagers need a different interpretation using age and sex, so this adult table should not be applied to them. [CDC: Adult BMI categories](https://www.cdc.gov/bmi/adult-calculator/bmi-categories.html)

## Put the number beside the rest of the picture

A clinician may consider medical history, health behaviors, examination findings, and laboratory results alongside BMI. Blood pressure and cholesterol are examples of information that the BMI calculation itself cannot provide. Someone with substantial muscle may fall into a higher BMI category without the calculation being able to explain why. [CDC: BMI questions](https://www.cdc.gov/bmi/faq/index.html)

You do not have to decide whether BMI is entirely useful or entirely useless before asking for a better explanation. A productive conversation can start with: “What does this result suggest in my situation, and what else are you considering?”

## Three questions to bring to a visit

Try writing down the question that matters most to you:

- “Are you concerned about my BMI itself, a change over time, or another finding?”
- “What additional information would help us understand my health?”
- “What are we trying to improve, and how will we know whether the plan is helping?”

These are conversation prompts, not a test you have to pass. You can also ask your clinician to explain an unfamiliar category in plain language.

The number in your chart deserves context. Ask for the explanation that connects it to your actual health, your concerns, and the decisions you are making together.

# What Is “Food Noise,” and Why Do People Talk About It?

Planning dinner is ordinary. So is looking forward to a favorite meal. But some people describe thoughts about food that keep interrupting the rest of the day: what to eat next, whether to eat, how to resist eating, or what they wish they had not eaten.

“Food noise” has become a popular name for that experience. It can give people language for something they struggled to explain. It can also become confusing when every craving or hungry afternoon gets placed under the same label.

Researchers are still working out how to define and measure it.

## A useful description, with boundaries still being studied

A 2025 expert paper proposed describing food noise in terms of unwanted, persistent food-related thoughts that interfere with everyday life. The work, funded by the telehealth company Ro, also explored ways to measure the experience. [The food-noise definition paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41387-025-00382-x).

A later theoretical review emphasized how much remains uncertain, including the causes of food noise and how treatments might change it. The review considered several possible explanations rather than identifying a single established mechanism. [Food noise: a theoretical review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42772688/).

It is therefore better understood as an emerging research concept and a description of experience than as a diagnosis you can confirm from a social-media quiz.

## Hunger, enjoyment, and distress are different

You can be hungry without spending hours preoccupied with food. You can enjoy cooking, plan a celebration meal, or notice a bakery without that experience being a problem.

The useful questions concern how intrusive the thoughts feel and what they interfere with. Can you return your attention to work or a conversation? Do food decisions take up time you wish you could spend elsewhere? Does the experience feel distressing?

These questions can help describe the issue to a professional. They are not a diagnostic test or a score that determines whether you should receive medication.

It is also worth describing the circumstances. Thoughts that become intense after a day of missed meals are a different starting point for a conversation from thoughts that feel relentless even when you are eating regularly. The label alone does not explain either experience.

## Why GLP-1 medicines entered the conversation

People taking GLP-1 medicines have reported changes in hunger, cravings, and the mental attention given to food. Researchers are studying those reports, but different studies measure different things.

In the 2026 INFORM survey, 550 US adults taking injectable semaglutide recalled their food-related thoughts before treatment and reported their current experience. Responses suggested less food noise after starting treatment. Because the comparison relied on recollection and had no randomized control group, it cannot prove that medication caused all of the reported change. Novo Nordisk employees were among the authors, and the company paid for the analysis. [INFORM survey](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42217114/).

That distinction does not invalidate someone’s relief. It matters when moving from “this is what I experienced” to “this will happen for everyone.”

The presence or absence of that feeling is also not a stand-alone way to judge whether a treatment is appropriate or working. Medication decisions need the broader health picture.

## Food noise is not another name for binge eating disorder

Binge eating disorder involves recurring episodes of eating unusually large amounts with a sense of losing control. Food-related preoccupation and binge eating can be part of the same person’s experience, but the terms do not mean the same thing.

The [NIDDK’s explanation of binge eating disorder](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/weight-management/binge-eating-disorder/definition-facts) describes it as a condition that warrants assessment. It can affect people across body sizes, and most people with obesity do not have it.

If your concerns include loss-of-control eating, purging, severe restriction, or substantial distress, describe those directly to a healthcare professional. Calling everything food noise can make it harder to identify the help you actually need.

## You do not need the perfect term to ask for help

A brief account of an ordinary day may be more useful than adopting a label. Explain when the thoughts appear, how they feel, whether you have been able to eat regularly, and what they prevent you from doing.

You might say, “I spend much of the afternoon thinking about what I will eat, and it is hard to focus,” or “I am constantly negotiating with myself about food.” These are examples of ways to describe an experience, not patient quotations.

The aim is to make the problem understandable. You do not have to prove that your thoughts meet an internet definition before they deserve attention.

articles.content:
# What Is Retatrutide, and Why Is It Getting Attention?

Retatrutide is an experimental medicine being studied for obesity and other conditions. It has attracted attention for the amount of weight participants have lost in clinical trials and for an approach that acts on three hormone receptors. Eli Lilly, its developer, is studying it as a weekly injection. [Retatrutide overview](https://www.lilly.com/news/stories/what-to-know-about-retatrutide)

**As of October 19, 2026, retatrutide is not FDA-approved.** Its research results can help us understand a possible future treatment, but there is no approved retatrutide prescription available today. [FDA guidance](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fdas-concerns-unapproved-glp-1-drugs-used-weight-loss)

## What does “triple agonist” mean?

Hormones send signals by attaching to receptors on cells. An agonist is a substance that activates a receptor. Retatrutide is one molecule designed to activate receptors for three hormones: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. That is why researchers call it a triple agonist. You may also encounter the nickname “GLP-3,” but that is not its scientific classification. [How retatrutide is described](https://www.lilly.com/news/stories/what-to-know-about-retatrutide)

The glucagon component is part of the scientific interest. In early experiments in mice, retatrutide's effects included eating less and using more energy, with glucagon-receptor activity contributing to the energy-use effect. These findings helped explain the rationale for developing the medicine. They do not establish how much extra energy a person would use or prove that three targets must work better than two. [Original development research](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35985340/)

For that, researchers need human trials that measure benefits and risks together.

## The weight-loss results behind the attention

The Phase 3 TRIUMPH-1 study randomly assigned 2,339 adults without diabetes to retatrutide or placebo for 80 weeks. Participants had obesity or overweight with a weight-related condition. The trial was funded by Lilly, and its main report was published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in September 2026. [Published study abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42814954/), [study population](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lillys-triple-agonist-retatrutide-delivered-powerful-weight-loss-in-pivotal-phase-3-obesity-trial-302778859.html)

In the analysis that accounted for participants regardless of whether they stayed on treatment, the highest-dose group, assigned 12 mg weekly, lost an estimated average of **25.0% of starting body weight**, compared with **3.9% with placebo**. The lower-dose groups also lost weight, with smaller average reductions. These are study results, not recommended doses or predictions for an individual. [TRIUMPH-1 results](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42814954/)

Losing roughly a quarter of starting weight explains why this research has drawn interest. Understanding the result also means looking at who was studied, how long treatment lasted, and which analysis produced the number.

## Why some headlines say 28.3%

Lilly also reported a 28.3% average reduction for the highest-dose group, versus 2.2% with placebo, using a different analysis. It estimates what would happen if participants stayed on the study treatment without starting prohibited weight-management treatments. The 25.0% estimate counts outcomes regardless of whether participants discontinued the study medicine or started other weight-management treatments. [Lilly's results and analysis definitions](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lillys-triple-agonist-retatrutide-delivered-powerful-weight-loss-in-pivotal-phase-3-obesity-trial-302778859.html)

Both analyses can be informative. The difference is a reason to read beyond the largest number in a headline. Neither tells you what your own result would be.

## Side effects are part of the result

Lilly reported nausea, diarrhea, constipation, and vomiting among the common adverse events in TRIUMPH-1. It also reported dysesthesia—unusual or unpleasant sensations, such as altered skin sensitivity. In the highest-dose group, 11.3% stopped treatment because of adverse events, compared with 4.9% receiving placebo. [Reported safety findings](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lillys-triple-agonist-retatrutide-delivered-powerful-weight-loss-in-pivotal-phase-3-obesity-trial-302778859.html)

Those experiences matter alongside the average weight loss. A treatment's usefulness depends partly on whether people can continue it, and an encouraging trial cannot rule out every uncommon or long-term risk. Retatrutide's safety is still being evaluated; there is no FDA-approved prescribing label that settles its uses, precautions, and dosing. [Current development status](https://www.lilly.com/news/stories/what-to-know-about-retatrutide)

## Is it better than tirzepatide?

TRIUMPH-1 compared retatrutide with placebo. It did not test retatrutide against tirzepatide or semaglutide. Putting percentages from separate trials next to each other does not create a direct comparison: the participants, duration, doses, and analysis can differ. [TRIUMPH-1 design](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42814954/)

A separate trial, TRIUMPH-5, is comparing retatrutide with tirzepatide. When checked on October 19, 2026, its registry listed it as active, with enrollment closed and no results posted. That comparison is one of the developments to watch as the evidence grows. [TRIUMPH-5 registry](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06662383?intr=retatrutide&tab=results)

## What about retatrutide offered online?

A website offering retatrutide does not mean it has become an approved treatment. FDA states that retatrutide cannot be used in compounding under federal law and warns against products sold to consumers under labels such as “for research purposes.” Their quality is unknown. [FDA guidance](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fdas-concerns-unapproved-glp-1-drugs-used-weight-loss)

Lilly says access to its investigational medicine is through its clinical trials. Participation depends on a study's eligibility requirements and whether it is recruiting. [Developer's access information](https://www.lilly.com/news/stories/what-to-know-about-retatrutide), [example trial requirements](https://trials.lilly.com/en-US/trial/549215)

If you are considering weight treatment now, a clinician can help you discuss the options already available and what fits your health history. Retatrutide is worth following as research develops. A future treatment possibility does not have to put today's care conversation on hold.
